headline: GM pays $220M to settle claims of selling drivers’ private data
summary: General Motors will pay $220 million to 36 states to resolve allegations that it illegally sold drivers’ private behavior and location information to data brokers.
details: General Motors has agreed to a $220 million settlement with 36 states to resolve allegations that it illegally sold drivers’ private behavior and location information to data brokers. This settlement requires GM to obtain drivers’ express consent before collecting or sharing their driving and location data.

The agreement settles a lawsuit brought by a coalition of attorneys general, alleging GM sold driver data to brokers who then sold it to insurance providers. This information could have impacted customers' insurance rates.
GM stated that this agreement addresses its "Smart Driver" product, which was discontinued in 2024. The company is committed to being clear about data usage, protection, and customer choices.

The settlement mandates that GM undergo third-party assessments of its compliance with its privacy program. This follows previous agreements with California and the Federal Trade Commission, which also required greater transparency and explicit consent for data collection.

GM has emphasized its commitment to privacy, stating it will no longer sell vehicle information tied to an individual, their location, or driving habits. However, anonymized data not linked to individuals may still be shared with partners.

This settlement occurs as vehicles become more sensor-laden and software-centric. GM is integrating features like a personal AI assistant into its OnStar service, with enhanced privacy controls and encryption for connected camera recordings.

headline: Reddit requires login for most content as AI impacts search
summary: The popular forum is changing its access policy, making it harder for AI models to scrape its vast data stores.
details: Reddit has announced a significant policy change that will soon require users to be logged in to view most of its content. This move aims to curb the rampant scraping of its data by AI companies.
The platform's vast repository of user-generated content has been a prime target for AI model training. By enforcing logins, Reddit hopes to regain control over how its data is accessed and utilized.

This decision comes as AI-driven search engines and tools increasingly rely on publicly available web data. Reddit's extensive archives are a rich source of information, making this a strategic move to protect its intellectual property and user privacy.

While the exact implementation details are still emerging, the change signals a broader trend of platforms reassessing data access in the age of AI. Users will need an account to participate and view content, impacting anonymous browsing.
